theory.overview: The key exchange problem haunted cryptography for millennia: how do two parties establish a shared secret over an insecure channel without meeting in person? In 1976, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman revolutionized cryptography with their elegant solution—two parties can derive an identical shared secret by exchanging public values while keeping private values secret. This breakthrough enabled secure internet communication, allowing strangers to establish encrypted connections without pre-shared keys. The Diffie-Hellman protocol, combined with RSA for authentication, powers the TLS handshake securing every HTTPS connection. Understanding key exchange is crucial because it explains how your browser establishes secure connections to websites you've never visited before.

sections.title: The Key Distribution Problem
sections.content: Before 1976, secure communication required physically exchanging keys. Military organizations used couriers with briefcases chained to their wrists; banks required in-person key setup. This was impractical for the emerging internet where millions of users needed secure connections with servers they'd never physically contact. Symmetric encryption provided speed and strength, but required shared secrets. Public key cryptography solved the problem by allowing parties to exchange public information that, combined with private secrets, generates identical shared keys. This is the foundation of modern secure communication.
keyPoints: Internet scale: Millions of parties, no prior contact
Solution: Mathematical key agreement over public channels
Result: Shared secret without transmitting the secret

sections.title: Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange
sections.content: Diffie-Hellman uses modular arithmetic in finite fields. Both parties agree on public parameters: a large prime p and a generator g (typically 2 or 5). Alice chooses private secret a, computes public A = g^a mod p. Bob chooses private secret b, computes public B = g^b mod p. They exchange A and B publicly. Alice computes shared secret s = B^a mod p = (g^b)^a mod p = g^(ba) mod p. Bob computes s = A^b mod p = (g^a)^b mod p = g^(ab) mod p. By the laws of exponents, both arrive at the same secret g^(ab) mod p, despite never transmitting it. An eavesdropper seeing A, B, g, p cannot compute g^(ab) without solving the discrete logarithm problem.
keyPoints: Public parameters: prime p, generator g
Private secrets: Alice's a, Bob's b
Public exchange: A = g^a, B = g^b
Shared secret: s = g^(ab) mod p

sections.title: Discrete Logarithm Problem
sections.content: Diffie-Hellman security rests on the discrete logarithm problem: given g, p, and g^x mod p, finding x is computationally infeasible for large p. Computing g^x (modular exponentiation) is fast using square-and-multiply. But reversing it—finding x given g^x—requires either trying all possibilities (infeasible for 2048-bit p) or using specialized algorithms like Number Field Sieve that still require enormous computation. The best known algorithms have sub-exponential complexity, meaning doubling key size makes attacks disproportionately harder. Current recommendations: use 2048-bit or larger primes, or better yet, elliptic curve variants (ECDH) providing equivalent security with smaller keys.
keyPoints: Forward: g^x mod p is fast to compute
Reverse: Finding x from g^x is hard
Best attack: General Number Field Sieve
ECDH: Same security, smaller keys (256-bit ≈ 3072-bit DH)

sections.title: Ephemeral Keys and Perfect Forward Secrecy
sections.content: Standard DH using static keys provides no forward secrecy—if an attacker records traffic and later steals a private key, they can retroactively decrypt all past communications. The solution: ephemeral Diffie-Hellman (DHE) where parties generate new key pairs for each session. After deriving the shared secret, they discard the private keys. Even if long-term authentication keys are compromised later, past session keys cannot be recovered because the ephemeral private keys are gone. This is called Perfect Forward Secrecy (PFS). Modern TLS 1.3 mandates ephemeral key exchange, ensuring that even certificate private key compromises cannot decrypt historical traffic.
keyPoints: Static DH: Compromised key decrypts all past traffic
Ephemeral DH: New key pair per session
Perfect Forward Secrecy: Past sessions safe even if keys stolen

steps.description: Bob chooses private secret b=15, computes public B = g^b mod p.

steps.title: Exchange Public Values
steps.description: Alice and Bob exchange public values A and B over the public channel. Eve sees these but cannot compute the secret.

steps.title: Alice Computes Shared Secret
steps.description: Alice uses her private key a and Bob's public key B to compute s = B^a mod p.

steps.title: Bob Computes Shared Secret
steps.description: Bob uses his private key b and Alice's public key A to compute s = A^b mod p.

steps.title: Shared Secret Established
steps.description: Both parties have derived the same shared secret s=2 without transmitting it. This becomes their symmetric key for AES encryption.

practiceProblems.title: DH Parameter Agreement
practiceProblems.description: Using p=17, g=3, Alice's a=5, Bob's b=7, what shared secret is computed?

solution.explanation: A=3^5 mod 17=5, B=3^7 mod 17=11, s=11^5 mod 17=14 or s=5^7 mod 17=14. Both compute same secret.

practiceProblems.title: Security of Small Primes
practiceProblems.description: Why is using a small prime like p=23 insecure for real DH key exchange?
practiceProblems.latex: \text{Brute force on discrete log with small } p
hints: Discrete log is hard for large p only

solution.answer: With small primes, brute force attacks on the discrete logarithm are trivial
solution.explanation: For p=23, an attacker can try all 22 possible values for the private key. Modern DH uses 2048-bit primes (primes with ~600 decimal digits) where brute force is impossible.

practiceProblems.title: Eavesdropper's Challenge
practiceProblems.description: Eve sees g=5, p=23, A=8, B=19. Can she compute the shared secret?
practiceProblems.latex: \text{Given } g, p, g^a, g^b \text{ - find } g^{ab}
hints: Eve needs to find a from 5^a mod 23 = 8
This is the discrete logarithm problem

solution.answer: No, computing the shared secret requires solving the discrete logarithm problem
solution.explanation: Eve knows g, p, g^a=8, g^b=19. To find g^(ab), she needs to find a such that 5^a ≡ 8 (mod 23), which requires solving the discrete logarithm. For large p, this is computationally infeasible.

practiceProblems.title: Perfect Forward Secrecy
practiceProblems.description: Alice and Bob use ephemeral DH for a session, then delete their private keys. A year later, an attacker steals both of their long-term authentication keys. Can the attacker decrypt the session?
hints: Ephemeral keys were deleted after session
Only ephemeral keys can compute the session secret
Long-term keys are for authentication only

solution.answer: No, the session remains secure because the ephemeral private keys were destroyed
solution.explanation: This is Perfect Forward Secrecy. Since Alice and Bob deleted their ephemeral private keys after deriving the shared secret, those keys cannot be stolen later. The long-term authentication keys cannot reconstruct the session key.

practiceProblems.title: Man-in-the-Middle Attack
practiceProblems.description: Why is raw DH vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks, and how do we prevent this?
practiceProblems.latex: \text{MITM: Mallory intercepts and replaces public keys}
hints: DH provides no authentication by itself
Mallory can establish separate secrets with each party

solution.answer: Raw DH is vulnerable because there's no authentication; we prevent it by signing DH public keys with RSA/ECDSA certificates
solution.explanation: In a MITM attack, Mallory intercepts Alice's public key, sends her own to Bob, and vice versa. She establishes one shared secret with Alice and another with Bob, decrypting and re-encrypting all traffic. TLS prevents this by having servers sign their DH public key with their certificate's private key, proving their identity.

practiceProblems.title: ECDH Comparison
practiceProblems.description: Elliptic Curve DH with 256-bit curves provides equivalent security to standard DH with what key size?
hints: Elliptic curve discrete log is harder than integer discrete log

solution.explanation: 256-bit ECDH provides approximately 128-bit security, equivalent to 3072-bit classical DH. This is because the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem is harder than the integer discrete logarithm problem, allowing smaller keys for equivalent security.

snippets.title: Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange
snippets.code:
import random

def mod_exp(base, exp, mod):
    """Fast modular exponentiation"""
    result = 1
    base = base % mod
    while exp > 0:
        if exp % 2 == 1:
            result = (result * base) % mod
        exp = exp >> 1
        base = (base * base) % mod
    return result

# Public parameters (small example - use large primes in practice)
p = 23  # Prime
g = 5   # Generator

# Alice's keys
a = 6  # Alice's private key
A = mod_exp(g, a, p)  # Alice's public key

# Bob's keys
b = 15  # Bob's private key
B = mod_exp(g, b, p)  # Bob's public key

# Key exchange
s_alice = mod_exp(B, a, p)  # Alice computes: B^a mod p
s_bob = mod_exp(A, b, p)    # Bob computes: A^b mod p

print(f"Alice's secret: {s_alice}")  # Both should be 2
print(f"Bob's secret: {s_bob}")      # Both should be 2
print(f"Match: {s_alice == s_bob}")
